sections.overview: The kelp perch is a viviparous surfperch (family Embiotocidae) of the northeastern Pacific. Its range extends from British Columbia to Baja California.
sections.identification: It may reach about 22 cm total length and is olive-brown to coppery above the lateral line, often with dark pigment beneath individual scales and a paler lower flank.
sections.habitat: It lives among giant kelp, especially Macrocystis, and also uses eelgrass, surfgrass, rocky bottoms and sand channels, most often in shallow water.
sections.diet: It takes small mobile invertebrates, especially crustaceans living on kelp, and may pick external parasites from other fishes.
sections.behavior: Young fish gather in schools just below the kelp canopy, whereas older fish are more dispersed along the kelp fronds; summer aggregations are also reported.
sections.reproduction: Like other surfperches, it gives birth to live young after internal fertilization, rather than releasing free eggs for external fertilization.
sections.ecology: It is one of several kelp-associated surfperches, alongside Embiotoca lateralis and other Embiotocidae; those family relatives share live birth, but differ in body markings and preferred microhabitats.
sections.conservation: The IUCN lists it as Data Deficient: kelp declines are documented across parts of its range, but the effects on this fish’s total population remain poorly measured.
